claim: Nineteen healthy adults (12 females, 19–40 years, M = 26.95, SD = 7.63) with normal or corrected-to-normal vision participated in this study.
source: Nineteen healthy adults (12 females, 19–40 years, M = 26.95, SD = 7.63) with normal or corrected-to-normal vision participated in this study.
evidence: Direct statement about participant demographics in the Methods section.

claim: Participants were recruited via convenience sampling from students at Monash University.
source: They were recruited via convenience sampling from students at Monash University, provided written informed consent prior to taking part, and were paid 20 AUD per hr of their time (approximately 3 hr total).
evidence: Direct statement about recruitment method.

claim: Participants were paid 20 AUD per hour for approximately 3 hours total.
source: They were recruited via convenience sampling from students at Monash University, provided written informed consent prior to taking part, and were paid 20 AUD per hr of their time (approximately 3 hr total).
evidence: Direct statement about participant compensation.

claim: Participants with self-reported sensitivity to flickering stimuli were excluded.
source: Participants with self-reported sensitivity to flickering stimuli were excluded.
evidence: Direct statement about exclusion criteria.

claim: Ethics approval was obtained from the Monash University Human Research Ethics Committee (MUHREC #CF12/2542 - 2012001375).
source: Ethics approval was obtained from the Monash University Human Research Ethics Committee (MUHREC #CF12/2542 - 2012001375).
evidence: Direct statement about ethics approval.

claim: Participants sat approximately 50 cm from a computer monitor.
source: Participants sat approximately 50 cm from a computer monitor (size 29 × 51 cm, resolution 1080 × 1920 pixels, subtending 32 × 54° visual angle, refresh rate 60 Hz).
evidence: Direct statement about experimental setup.

claim: The computer monitor had a size of 29 × 51 cm, resolution of 1080 × 1920 pixels, subtending 32 × 54° visual angle, and refresh rate of 60 Hz.
source: Participants sat approximately 50 cm from a computer monitor (size 29 × 51 cm, resolution 1080 × 1920 pixels, subtending 32 × 54° visual angle, refresh rate 60 Hz).
evidence: Direct statement about monitor specifications.

claim: The background surrounding target stimuli was refreshed at a rate of 20 Hz.
source: The background surrounding our target stimuli (Figure 1) was refreshed at a rate of 20 Hz by randomly selecting one of 100, pre-calculated, random patterns generated at the start of the experiment.
evidence: Direct statement about background refresh rate.

claim: The random patterns were made up by dividing the screen into squares of 10 × 10 pixels (0.3 × 0.3° visual angle), with each square's luminance randomly set to either black or white.
source: The random patterns were made up by dividing the screen into squares of 10 × 10 pixels (0.3 × 0.3° visual angle), with each square's luminance randomly set to either black or white.
evidence: Direct statement about stimulus construction.

claim: A 5 mm (0.57° visual angle) diameter red dot served as a fixation point at the centre.
source: At the centre was a 5 mm (0.57° visual angle) diameter red dot serving as a fixation point.
evidence: Direct statement about fixation point.

claim: One circular target was presented in each of the four visual quadrants (top left, top right, bottom left, and bottom right).
source: One circular target was presented in each of the four visual quadrants (top left, top right, bottom left, and bottom right).
evidence: Direct statement about target locations.

claim: Targets subtended 6.08° visual angle in diameter.
source: Targets subtended 6.08° visual angle in diameter, within which the white background squares were instead colored as blue/purple (RGB value of 205, 205, 255).
evidence: Direct statement about target size.

claim: Target regions had an RGB value of 205, 205, 255 (blue/purple).
source: Targets subtended 6.08° visual angle in diameter, within which the white background squares were instead colored as blue/purple (RGB value of 205, 205, 255).
evidence: Direct statement about target color.

claim: There were no line-contours at target boundaries, as target boundaries were defined by the pixelated squares of the background they were overlaid on.
source: There were no line-contours at target boundaries, as target boundaries were defined by the pixelated squares of the background they were overlaid on (Figure 1c).
evidence: Direct statement about target boundary definition.

claim: During PFI, target regions became perceptually indistinguishable from the surrounding background texture.
source: As a result, during PFI, target regions became perceptually indistinguishable from the surrounding background texture.
evidence: Direct statement about perceptual outcome during PFI.

claim: The refresh rate of texture within the target regions was set to 15 Hz.
source: The refresh rate of texture within the target regions was set to 15 Hz, with target eccentricity individually calibrated per participant to evoke optimal PFI and SSVEP strength (see Figure 1c, and Pre-experiment SSVEP calibration of target eccentricity).
evidence: Direct statement about target refresh rate.

claim: Target eccentricity was individually calibrated per participant to evoke optimal PFI and SSVEP strength.
source: The refresh rate of texture within the target regions was set to 15 Hz, with target eccentricity individually calibrated per participant to evoke optimal PFI and SSVEP strength (see Figure 1c, and Pre-experiment SSVEP calibration of target eccentricity).
evidence: Direct statement about calibration procedure.

claim: EEG was recorded with 64 active electrodes arranged according to the international 10–10 system.
source: Throughout each session, EEG was recorded with 64 active electrodes arranged according to the international 10–10 system (BrainProducts, ActiCap RRID:SCR_009443).
evidence: Direct statement about EEG recording setup.

claim: Electrode impedances were kept below 10 kΩ prior to experimentation.
source: Electrode impedances were kept below 10 kΩ prior to experimentation, and recorded using the default reference (FCz) and ground electrode (AFz) via Brainvision (RRID:SCR_002356) recorder software (sampling rate = 1000 Hz, offline bandpass of 0.5–70 Hz).
evidence: Direct statement about electrode impedance threshold.

claim: EEG was recorded using the default reference (FCz) and ground electrode (AFz) via Brainvision recorder software with a sampling rate of 1000 Hz and offline bandpass of 0.5–70 Hz.
source: Electrode impedances were kept below 10 kΩ prior to experimentation, and recorded using the default reference (FCz) and ground electrode (AFz) via Brainvision (RRID:SCR_002356) recorder software (sampling rate = 1000 Hz, offline bandpass of 0.5–70 Hz).
evidence: Direct statement about EEG recording parameters.

claim: Targets were initially centred close to fixation at 4.3° visual angle in eccentricity measured from the fixation dot to the center of the target.
source: Targets were initially centred close to fixation (4.3° visual angle in eccentricity measured from the fixation dot to the center of the target).
evidence: Direct statement about initial target position.

claim: Target eccentricity was adjusted along the diagonal from 4.3 to 8.7° in steps of 0.4° depending on subjective reports.
source: Depending on their subjective reports, we adjusted the eccentricity of the targets along the diagonal (from 4.3 to 8.7°, in steps of 0.4°) so that their perceptual experience was described as 'appearing and disappearing often, for a few seconds at a time'.
evidence: Direct statement about calibration procedure.

claim: All participants reported that PFI occurred.
source: All participants reported that PFI occurred.
evidence: Direct statement about participant reports.

claim: For two participants, tagging was unsuccessful at all settings, and the largest and most central target position at which any PFI occurred was adopted.
source: In the absence of readily observable peaks in the real time EEG spectra, target eccentricity was reduced, and the process was repeated. If tagging was unsuccessful at all settings (n = 2), the largest and most central target position at which any PFI occurred was adopted.
evidence: Direct statement about exceptions in calibration.

claim: Participants were instructed to press keys 'A', 'Z', 'K', and 'M' on a traditional QWERTY keyboard, assigning them to the upper left, bottom left, upper right, and bottom right targets, respectively.
source: Specifically, they were instructed to press keys 'A', 'Z', 'K', and 'M' on a traditional QWERTY keyboard, assigning them to the upper left, bottom left, upper right, and bottom right targets, respectively.
evidence: Direct statement about response mapping.

claim: Each participant completed one 60 s practice trial, followed by 48 self-paced, experimental trials which were also one minute long.
source: After calibration, each participant completed one 60 s practice trial, followed by 48 self-paced, experimental trials which were also one minute long.
evidence: Direct statement about experimental procedure.

claim: Participants took mandatory breaks of 3–5 min every 12 trials, while EEG recordings were paused and channel impedances were monitored.
source: Participants took mandatory breaks of 3–5 min every 12 trials, while EEG recordings were paused and channel impedances were monitored.
evidence: Direct statement about break schedule.

claim: Each trial included one randomly generated PMD period of between 3.5 and 5 s (drawn from a uniform distribution), during which one to four targets were physically removed from the screen.
source: Each trial included one randomly generated PMD period of between 3.5 and 5 s (drawn from a uniform distribution), during which one to four targets were physically removed from the screen.
evidence: Direct statement about PMD periods.

claim: Participants were not informed of physical disappearance periods before the experiment.
source: Participants were not informed of these physical disappearance periods before the experiment.
evidence: Direct statement about participant instructions.

claim: PMD did not occur in the first 10 s of each trial.
source: To mimic the frequency of genuine PFI, PMD did not occur in the first 10 s of each trial (Schieting and Spillmann, 1987).
evidence: Direct statement about PMD timing, supported by citation.

claim: Three participants were excluded for failing to identify PMD periods.
source: We excluded participants (n = 3, See Figure 1—figure supplement 1) with no PMD-onset reaction time in the first 2 s (i.e. [0, S+2]).
evidence: Direct statement about participant exclusion with reference to figure.

claim: For two of the excluded participants, it appeared that buttons were consistently released at PMD-onset rather than pressed as per instructions.
source: We note that for two of these participants, it appeared that buttons were consistently released at PMD-onset – potentially indicating buttons were released during PFI rather than pressed as per instructions.
evidence: Direct statement about participant behavior.

claim: For the remaining participants (N=16), the mean reaction time to respond to PMD onsets was 0.68 s (SD = 0.31).
source: For the remaining participants, the mean reaction time to respond to PMD onsets, and thus the disappearance of a peripheral target was 0.68 s (SD = 0.31).
evidence: Direct statement about reaction time measurement.

claim: Overall, only 16 trials were rejected across 16 retained participants.
source: Figure 1—figure supplement 2c shows a histogram of the number of rejected trials per participant (overall, only 16 trials were rejected) across 16 retained participants.
evidence: Direct statement about trial rejection with reference to figure.

claim: Targets disappeared together more frequently than in isolation.
source: We first confirmed in our behavioral analysis that targets disappeared together more frequently than in isolation (see Supplementary results, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Direct statement about behavioral finding with reference to supplementary results.

claim: The duration of PFI increases with an increasing number of invisible targets.
source: Consistent with our prior work, we also replicate that the duration of PFI increases with an increasing number of invisible targets, strongly suggesting a facilitatory grouping mechanism across visual hemifields and target locations (Davidson et al., 2020).
evidence: Direct statement about behavioral finding with citation to prior work.

claim: The strength of target-specific neural responses increased prior to the subjective report of a target becoming invisible.
source: We found that the strength of target-specific neural responses increased prior to the subjective report of a target becoming invisible.
evidence: Direct statement about neural finding.

claim: The magnitudes of target-SNR time courses for disappearances versus reappearances differ significantly from −0.74 s before, through to 1.53 s after subjective report (pcluster <0.001).
source: The magnitudes of each time course differ significantly from −0.74 s before, through to 1.53 s after subjective report (pcluster <0.001).
evidence: Direct statement about statistical finding.

claim: During PFI, target-SNR is negatively correlated with the contents of conscious perception; when a target disappears, target-SNR increases.
source: During this period, target-SNR is negatively correlated with the contents of conscious perception during PFI; when a target disappears, target-SNR increases.
evidence: Direct statement about correlation between neural activity and perception.

claim: Increases in the amount of PFI (i.e., decreased visibility) significantly increased target-SNR (linear-mixed effects, likelihood ratio test: χ2(1)=11.60, p=6.58 × 10−4).
source: We found that increases in the amount of PFI (i.e., decreased visibility) significantly increased target-SNR (linear-mixed effects, likelihood ratio test: χ2(1)=11.60, p=6.58 × 10−4; Figure 2c -blue), confirming that target-SNR increased as a measure of target invisibility during PFI.
evidence: Direct statement about statistical finding with test results.

claim: Surround-SNR increased during the filling-in of targets, compared to their reappearance, from −0.99 to 1.28 s around report (pcluster <0.001).
source: Unlike target-SNR, surround-SNR tracked the contents of phenomenology; it increased during the filling-in of targets, compared to their reappearance, from −0.99 to 1.28 s around report (pcluster <0.001; Figure 2d), and it linearly increased with the amount of PFI (χ2(1)=19.63, p=9.41 × 10−6; Figure 2f -black).
evidence: Direct statement about statistical finding.

claim: Surround-SNR linearly increased with the amount of PFI (χ2(1)=19.63, p=9.41 × 10−6).
source: Unlike target-SNR, surround-SNR tracked the contents of phenomenology; it increased during the filling-in of targets, compared to their reappearance, from −0.99 to 1.28 s around report (pcluster <0.001; Figure 2d), and it linearly increased with the amount of PFI (χ2(1)=19.63, p=9.41 × 10−6; Figure 2f -black).
evidence: Direct statement about statistical finding.

claim: Target and surround signals are positively correlated during PFI, and positively correlated with the fluctuating number of invisible targets.
source: Thus, target and surround signals are positively correlated during PFI, and positively correlated with the fluctuating number of invisible targets.
evidence: Direct statement summarizing correlation findings.

claim: During PMD, target-SNR significantly decreased (χ2(1)=18.35, p=1.84 × 10−5), rather than increased as during PFI.
source: During PMD, target-SNR significantly decreased (χ2(1)=18.35, p=1.84 × 10−5; Figure 2c -red), rather than increased as during PFI.
evidence: Direct statement about statistical finding comparing PMD to PFI.

claim: Surround-SNR significantly increased with increasing amounts of PMD (χ2(1)=7.37, p=0.007).
source: No dissociation between PMD and PFI periods was observed for surround-SNR, which significantly increased with increasing amounts of PMD (χ2(1)=7.37, p=0.007; Figure 2f -red), as it did for PFI.
evidence: Direct statement about statistical finding.

claim: Only during PFI, when periods of invisibility were endogenously generated, did the specifically target-sensitive neural responses increase in SNR.
source: This pattern of results confirms that only during PFI, when periods of invisibility were endogenously generated, did the specifically target-sensitive neural responses increase in SNR.
evidence: Direct statement summarizing the contrast between PFI and PMD.

claim: A significant difference was confirmed between baseline alpha amplitude (averaged −2.5 to −1.5 s prior to button press), and alpha amplitude evoked during PFI (pcluster = 0.004, electrode-time cluster corrected).
source: With a cluster-based permutation test (Maris and Oostenveld, 2007; see Materials and methods), we confirmed a significant difference between baseline alpha amplitude (averaged −2.5 to −1.5 s prior to button press), and alpha amplitude evoked during PFI (Figure 3b; pcluster = 0.004, electrode-time cluster corrected).
evidence: Direct statement about statistical finding with citation to method.

claim: The PFI-evoked alpha difference corresponded to a centro-parietal cluster of electrodes, and reduction in alpha during PFI from −0.14 s through to 0.65 s after button press.
source: This condition difference corresponded to a centro-parietal cluster of electrodes, and reduction in alpha during PFI from −0.14 s through to 0.65 s after button press.
evidence: Direct statement about spatial and temporal characteristics of alpha finding.

claim: During PMD, a smaller centro-parietal cluster of electrodes, and briefer later latency range (0.35 to 0.41 s) was significant (pcluster = 0.006, electrode-time cluster corrected).
source: During PMD, a smaller centro-parietal cluster of electrodes, and briefer later latency range (0.35 to 0.41 s) was significant (Figure 3c; pcluster = 0.006, electrode-time cluster corrected).
evidence: Direct statement about statistical finding for PMD.

claim: Alpha amplitude significantly reduced from approximately −0.77 to 1.58 s during PFI (p<0.011 at FDR q = 0.05).
source: When comparing the evoked alpha during PFI and PMD to the prestimulus baseline, alpha amplitude significantly reduced from approximately −0.77 to 1.58 s during PFI (Figure 3d; p<0.011 at FDR q = 0.05).
evidence: Direct statement about statistical finding with FDR correction.

claim: During PMD, no significant reduction in alpha was retained after false-discovery rate corrections (FDR q = 0.05).
source: During PMD, no significant reduction in alpha was retained after false-discovery rate corrections (FDR q = 0.05).
evidence: Direct statement about lack of significant finding after correction.

claim: Across participants, mean evoked alpha suppression negatively correlated with the strength of target-SNR during PFI (r = −0.58, p=0.019).
source: Across participants, mean evoked alpha suppression also negatively correlated with the strength of target-SNR during PFI (r = −0.58, p=0.019, Figure 3e).
evidence: Direct statement about correlation finding.

claim: No correlation was found between evoked alpha reductions and target-SNR during PMD (r = −0.34, p=0.22).
source: No correlation was found between evoked alpha reductions and target-SNR during PMD (r = −0.34, p=0.22).
evidence: Direct statement about lack of correlation.

claim: Changes to surround-SNR preceded changes to target-SNR by approximately 200 ms.
source: As Figure 2 shows, after overlaying the SNR time courses for perceptual disappearance and reappearance, the latency of significant changes to target (f1) and surround (f2) SNR differed substantially. Specifically, changes to surround-SNR preceded changes to target-SNR by approximately 200 ms (one time-step in our moving window spectrogram analysis).
evidence: Direct statement about temporal relationship with reference to figure.

claim: The magnitude of IM-SNR transiently peaked prior to a perceptual disappearance.
source: We also observed that the magnitude of IM-SNR transiently peaked prior to a perceptual disappearance, although the overall strength of the IM component was substantially weaker (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Direct statement about IM-SNR timing with reference to figure.

claim: During PFI, the median first significant time-point for f2 (median = −1.22 s, SD = −0.02) preceded f1 (median = −0.43 s; SD = 0.26 s).
source: During PFI, the median first significant time-point for f2 (median = −1.22 s, SD = −0.02) preceded f1 (median = −0.43 s; SD = 0.26 s).
evidence: Direct statement about jackknife analysis results.

claim: For every jackknifed subsample, changes in f2 always preceded f1, and the difference between these distributions was significant (paired t-test, t(15) = 9.36, p=1.94 × 10-7; Wilcoxon signed-rank test, z = 3.52, p=4.38 × 10−4).
source: Importantly, for every jackknifed subsample, changes in f2 always preceded f1, and the difference between these distributions was significant (paired t-test, t(15) = 9.36, p=1.94 × 10-7; Wilcoxon signed-rank test, z = 3.52, p=4.38 × 10−4).
evidence: Direct statement about statistical finding with multiple tests.

claim: No significant cluster was retained for IM-SNR on 43% of jackknifed subsamples.
source: The timing of changes in IM-SNR was not as statistically reliable. No significant cluster was retained on 43% of our jackknifed subsamples, which we attribute to the reduced strength of IM-SNR.
evidence: Direct statement about reliability of IM-SNR finding.

claim: Changes in IM SNR occurred between the times observed for the fundamental frequencies (median = −0.83 s, SD = 0.09).
source: Notably, however, and despite this reduced strength, changes in IM SNR occurred between the times observed for the fundamental frequencies (median = −0.83 s, SD = 0.09).
evidence: Direct statement about IM-SNR timing.

claim: During PMD periods, the median first significant time-point for target-SNR (median = −0.52, SD = 0.02) preceded surround-SNR (median = −0.10, SD = 0.10).
source: During PMD periods, the pattern between the target and surround-SNR was reversed. The median first significant time-point for target-SNR (median = −0.52, SD = 0.02) preceded surround-SNR (median = −0.10, SD = 0.10).
evidence: Direct statement about PMD timing pattern.

claim: The reversal in timing between target and surround-SNR during PMD was present on every jackknifed subsample (paired t-test, t(15) = −16.64, p=4.48 × 10−11; Wilcoxon signed-rank test, z = 3.52, p=4.38 × 10−4).
source: This reversal was present on every jackknifed subsample (paired t-test, t(15) = −16.64, p=4.48 × 10−11; Wilcoxon signed-rank test, z = 3.52, p=4.38 × 10−4).
evidence: Direct statement about statistical finding with multiple tests.

claim: During PMD, changes to the magnitude of IM-SNR occurred after button press (median = 0.73, SD = 0.20), and after changes to the target and surround-SNR on every subsample.
source: Unlike during PFI periods, changes to the magnitude of IM-SNR occurred after button press (median = 0.73, SD = 0.20), and after changes to the target and surround-SNR on every subsample.
evidence: Direct statement about IM-SNR timing during PMD.

claim: Target-SNR latencies were equivalent between PFI and PMD conditions (t(15) = −1.56, p=0.14), occurring 500 ms prior to button press.
source: Indeed, target-SNR latencies were equivalent between PFI and PMD conditions (t(15) = −1.56, p=0.14), occurring 500 ms prior to button press.
evidence: Direct statement about statistical comparison.

claim: SSVEPs have been extensively used as the neural correlates of visual consciousness, predominantly when combined with binocular rivalry.
source: Importantly, SSVEPs have been extensively used as the neural correlates of visual consciousness, predominantly when combined with binocular rivalry (Brown and Norcia, 1997; Cobb et al., 1967; Katyal et al., 2016; Lansing, 1964; Tononi et al., 1998; Zhang et al., 2011).
evidence: Direct statement about prior use of SSVEPs with multiple citations.

claim: During binocular rivalry, the relative strength of frequency-tagged activity positively correlates with behavioral reports of the dominant image.
source: When two flickering stimuli compete during rivalry, the relative strength of frequency-tagged activity positively correlates with behavioral reports of the dominant image (Bock et al., 2019; Brown and Norcia, 1997; Cosmelli et al., 2004; Jamison et al., 2015; Kamphuisen et al., 2008; Katyal et al., 2016; Lansing, 1964; Lawwill and Biersdorf, 1968; Roy et al., 2017; Srinivasan et al., 1999; Sutoyo and Srinivasan, 2009; Tononi et al., 1998; Zhang et al., 2011).
evidence: Direct statement about prior findings with extensive citations.

claim: SSVEPs have been employed as a measure of selective attention, which increases the strength of SSVEP responses.
source: In a largely separate and parallel body of literature, SSVEPs have also been employed as a measure of selective attention, which increases the strength of SSVEP responses (Morgan et al., 1996; Müller et al., 2006, Müller et al., 1998; Müller and Hillyard, 2000; Müller and Hübner, 2002; Walter et al., 2012).
evidence: Direct statement about prior findings with citations.

claim: An increase in SSVEP strength when stimuli are attended also occurs when flickering items are presented simultaneously in close proximity.
source: Notably, an increase in SSVEP strength when stimuli are attended also occurs when flickering items are presented simultaneously in close proximity (Andersen et al., 2008; Müller et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2007).
evidence: Direct statement about prior findings with citations.

claim: Smout and Mattingley (2018) demonstrated that allocating spatial attention to the side of an invisible SSVEP-inducing stimulus embedded in noise enhanced the strength of the SSVEP.
source: In their recent study, Smout and Mattingley, 2018, further demonstrated the potential of the SSVEP to dissociate the neural effects of attention from consciousness. Specifically, although their participants were unaware of an SSVEP-inducing stimulus embedded in noise, allocating spatial attention to the side of the invisible stimulus enhanced the strength of the SSVEP (Smout and Mattingley, 2018).
evidence: Direct statement about prior study findings with citation.

claim: Directing attention toward targets in the visual periphery facilitates perceptual disappearance during PFI.
source: In the behavioral and neuronal study of consciousness and attention, PFI has an unusual and potentially very revealing property: directing attention toward targets in the visual periphery facilitates perceptual disappearance (De Weerd et al., 2006; Lou, 1999).
evidence: Direct statement about PFI property with citations.

claim: PFI occurs regularly in normal vision, as in the visual areas that are occluded by the blindspot, and the blood vessels in the retina.
source: For example, compared to more widely studied forms of multistable stimuli that require inter-ocular suppression, PFI occurs regularly in normal vision (Anstis and Greenlee, 2014; De Weerd, 2006; Durgin et al., 1995), as in the visual areas that are occluded by the blindspot, and the blood vessels in the retina (Komatsu, 2006).
evidence: Direct statement about PFI occurrence with citations.

claim: Event-related reductions in alpha are commonly interpreted as a measure of enhanced cortical excitability under top-down control.
source: Event-related reductions in alpha are commonly interpreted as a measure of enhanced cortical excitability under top-down control (Halgren et al., 2019; Jensen and Mazaheri, 2010), and correlate with the subjective intensity of attentional effort (Macdonald et al., 2011).
evidence: Direct statement about alpha interpretation with citations.

claim: Evoked alpha responses are frequently regarded as a measure of attention.
source: Evoked alpha responses are thus frequently regarded as a measure of attention (Foxe et al., 1998; Foxe and Snyder, 2011; Gould et al., 2011; Sokoliuk et al., 2019; Worden et al., 2000).
evidence: Direct statement about alpha interpretation with citations.

claim: Intermodulation components have been proposed to index interactions between stimulus representations.
source: These IM components have been proposed to index interactions between stimulus representations (Ales et al., 2012; Alp et al., 2016; Boremanse et al., 2013; Gordon et al., 2017; Gundlach and Müller, 2013), which peak prior to a perceptual change during binocular rivalry (Katyal et al., 2016), and which increase when stimuli are attended (Gordon et al., 2017; Kim et al., 2017; Kim and Verghese, 2012).
evidence: Direct statement about IM components with citations.

claim: The most prominent model of PFI proposes that interactions in the early retinotopic cortex are responsible for disappearances.
source: To explain the phenomenon of PFI, the most prominent model proposes that interactions in the early retinotopic cortex are responsible for disappearances (Pessoa et al., 1998; Spillmann and De Weerd, 2003, for rejections on philosophical grounds, see Dennett, 1991; O'Regan, 1992; O'Regan and Noë, 2001).
evidence: Direct statement about PFI model with citations.

claim: In the PFI model, a primary stage of seconds-long adaptation occurs in neural populations that are sensitive to the boundary between a target and background region.
source: In this model, a primary stage of seconds-long adaptation occurs in neural populations that are sensitive to the boundary between a target and background region.
evidence: Direct statement about model mechanism.

claim: The adaptation stage interacts with an interpolation of the surrounding visual features into the target region, likely achieved via the lateral spread of neural activity through horizontal connections between pyramidal cells.
source: This stage interacts with an interpolation of the surrounding visual features into the target region, likely achieved via the lateral spread of neural activity through horizontal connections between pyramidal cells (for review; Spillmann and De Weerd, 2003).
evidence: Direct statement about model mechanism with citation.

claim: De Weerd et al. showed that monkey single-unit responses increased after several seconds to match the spike rate measured within the same receptive field when viewing only the homogenous texture.
source: Then, using the same apparatus, monkey single-unit responses were shown to increase after several seconds to match the spike rate measured within the same receptive field when viewing only the homogenous texture.
evidence: Direct statement about prior study findings.

claim: The timing of climbing activity in monkey neurons corresponded to the average timing of filling-in reported in humans, which has been interpreted in support of an active and early retinotopic filling-in mechanism.
source: As the timing of this climbing activity corresponded to the average timing of filling-in reported in humans, this has been interpreted in support of an active and early retinotopic filling-in mechanism.
evidence: Direct statement about interpretation of prior findings.

claim: Previous studies did not establish a tight correlation between neural activity and perceptual reports through trial-by-trial fluctuations or inter-individual variance.
source: The correspondence remains suggestive, however, because these previous studies did not establish a tight correlation between neural activity and perceptual reports through trial-by-trial fluctuations or inter-individual variance.
evidence: Direct statement critiquing prior studies.

claim: The current paradigm is able to provide new evidence in support of an interaction between the target and background regions, time-locked to behavioral reports in human participants.
source: By uniquely frequency-tagging both the target and surrounds, our paradigm is able to provide new evidence in support of an interaction between the target and background regions, time-locked to behavioral reports in human participants, whose neural activity and perceptual reports were obtained simultaneously.
evidence: Direct statement about contribution of current study.

claim: Previous work has analyzed SSVEPs evoked only by a single target during PFI, or only by the surrounding background, leaving the precise sequence of these neural activations unclear.
source: Previous work has analyzed SSVEPs evoked only by a single target during PFI (Weil et al., 2007), or only by the surrounding background (Davidson et al., 2020), leaving the precise sequence of these neural activations unclear.
evidence: Direct statement about limitations of prior work with citations.

claim: The temporal ordering of surround, IM, and target activations seems difficult to reconcile with a model of PFI which claims that interactions between stimulus representations are unnecessary to account for the phenomenology of filling-in.
source: This temporal ordering effect seems difficult to reconcile with a model of PFI, which claims that interactions between stimulus representations are unnecessary to account for the phenomenology of filling-in (Dennett, 1991; De Weerd et al., 2006; Kingdom and Moulden, 1988; Pessoa et al., 1998).
evidence: Direct statement about implications for models with citations.

claim: In the current display, target borders were continuously changed due to the dynamic texture that was shared by targets and surrounds, which may reduce boundary adaptation.
source: In our display, target borders were continuously changed due to the dynamic texture that was shared by targets and surrounds (Figure 1c). As a consequence, boundary adaptation may be reduced (Spillmann and Kurtenbach, 1992), and it remains possible that neurons higher in the visual hierarchy with a sensitivity to color (such as in V4) are the neural correlates of PFI in our paradigm.
evidence: Direct statement about stimulus design implications with citation.

claim: It remains possible that neurons higher in the visual hierarchy with a sensitivity to color (such as in V4) are the neural correlates of PFI in the current paradigm.
source: As a consequence, boundary adaptation may be reduced (Spillmann and Kurtenbach, 1992), and it remains possible that neurons higher in the visual hierarchy with a sensitivity to color (such as in V4) are the neural correlates of PFI in our paradigm.
evidence: Direct statement about possible neural mechanisms.

claim: First-order theories of conscious perception propose that the strength of activity within content-specific visual processing areas determines the vividness of that visual experience.
source: For example, first-order theories of conscious perception (Mehta and Mashour, 2013; Zeki, 2007) propose that the strength of activity within content-specific visual processing areas determines the vividness of that visual experience.
evidence: Direct statement about theoretical position with citations.

claim: The global neuronal workspace theory (GNWT) of consciousness considers stronger neural activation as a prerequisite to entry within the global neuronal workspace and subsequent conscious access.
source: Similarly, the global neuronal workspace theory (GNWT) of consciousness (Dehaene and Naccache, 2001; Mashour et al., 2020) also considers stronger neural activation as a prerequisite to entry within the global neuronal workspace and subsequent conscious access (van Vugt et al., 2018).
evidence: Direct statement about theoretical position with citations.

claim: Insofar as the strength of target SSVEP signals when measured with EEG may reflect the strength of target-specific spike activity in the sensory cortex, the current finding challenges theories that propose response strength is positively correlated with the vividness of conscious experience.
source: Insofar as the strength of target SSVEP signals when measured with EEG may reflect the strength of target-specific spike activity in the sensory cortex, our finding does challenge such theories that propose response strength is positively correlated with the vividness of conscious experience.
evidence: Direct statement about implications for theories.

claim: The exact mechanisms of SSVEP generation are not well understood.
source: Currently, however, the exact mechanisms of SSVEP generation are not well understood (Kawashima et al., 2020; Kim et al., 2017; Norcia et al., 2015; Notbohm et al., 2016; Rager and Singer, 1998; Salelkar and Ray, 2020), and future studies will be necessary to clarify their input.
evidence: Direct statement about current knowledge limitations with citations.

claim: There is precedent in the literature of a negative correlation between the magnitude of neural spiking and visibility, including single neuron spike-rates recorded during binocular rivalry.
source: It is important to acknowledge the precedent in the literature of a negative correlation between the magnitude of neural spiking and visibility. Prominent examples include single neuron spike-rates recorded during binocular rivalry (reviewed in Logothetis, 1998).
evidence: Direct statement about prior findings with citation.

claim: During binocular rivalry recording in macaques, 22% of the recorded neurons in V4 and MT were responsive, and of these, half showed enhanced firing rates when the preferred stimulus was dominant, while the other half showed enhanced firing rates when their preferred stimulus was suppressed.
source: In these studies, each neuron's receptive field and preferred stimuli was carefully mapped before a binocular rivalry session in macaques. During recording, 22% of the recorded neurons in V4 and MT were responsive during rivalry. Of these neurons, half showed enhanced firing rates when the preferred stimulus was dominant, while the other half showed enhanced firing rates when their preferred stimulus was suppressed (Logothetis, 1989a; Logothetis and Schall, 1989b).
evidence: Direct statement about prior findings with citations.

claim: Neurons in anti-correlation with the animals' perception counter the notion that the strength of activity early in the sensory cortex determines the contents of conscious perception.
source: These neurons in anti-correlation with the animals' perception counter the notion that the strength of activity early in the sensory cortex determines the contents of conscious perception.
evidence: Direct statement about implications of prior findings.

claim: Recurrent processing theory and integrated information theory propose that certain types of causal interactions underlie conscious phenomenology.
source: Meanwhile, there exists another family of theories that propose that certain types of causal interactions underlie conscious phenomenology, such as recurrent processing theory (Lamme, 2006; Lamme, 2014; Lamme and Roelfsema, 2000) and integrated information theory (Haun and Tononi, 2019; Tononi, 2004).
evidence: Direct statement about theoretical positions with citations.

claim: For recurrent processing theory and integrated information theory, it is not the strength, but the patterns of neuronal connectivity and their states that determine phenomenology as a whole.
source: For these theories, it is not the strength, but the patterns of neuronal connectivity and their states that determine phenomenology as a whole.
evidence: Direct statement about theoretical positions.

claim: The study shows increased neural responses to the disappearance of stimuli, which challenges long-held beliefs regarding a positive correlation between the strength of SSVEPs and visual phenomenology.
source: We show increased neural responses to the disappearance of stimuli, which challenges long-held beliefs regarding a positive correlation between the strength of SSVEPs and visual phenomenology.
evidence: Direct statement summarizing main finding and its implications.

claim: From indirect, yet convergent evidence, SSVEP strength in the current paradigm is more parsimoniously explained to reflect a neural correlate of attention.
source: From indirect, yet convergent evidence, we conclude that SSVEP strength in our paradigm is more parsimoniously explained to reflect a neural correlate of attention.
evidence: Direct statement of main conclusion based on multiple lines of evidence.

claim: The findings demonstrate the need to carefully re-examine previous uses of the SSVEP as a neural correlate of consciousness.
source: This demonstrates the need to carefully re-examine previous uses of the SSVEP as a neural correlate of consciousness, and positions the dynamic texture tagging technique as a promising method to deepen our understanding of SSVEP mechanisms, and open new lines of empirical enquiry in consciousness research.
evidence: Direct statement about implications for the field.

claim: The dynamic texture tagging technique is positioned as a promising method to deepen understanding of SSVEP mechanisms and open new lines of empirical enquiry in consciousness research.
source: This demonstrates the need to carefully re-examine previous uses of the SSVEP as a neural correlate of consciousness, and positions the dynamic texture tagging technique as a promising method to deepen our understanding of SSVEP mechanisms, and open new lines of empirical enquiry in consciousness research.
evidence: Direct statement about methodological contribution.

claim: Psychophysical studies of PFI have established that increased attention to targets which share colors or forms facilitates their disappearance.
source: First, psychophysical studies of PFI have established that increased attention to targets, which share colors or forms facilitates their disappearance (De Weerd et al., 2006; Lou, 1999).
evidence: Direct statement about prior findings with citations.

claim: The study capitalized on the finding that attention facilitates PFI by designing targets which shared color, form, and temporal flicker.
source: We capitalized on this result by designing targets which shared color, form, and temporal flicker, and replicate that these targets disappear together more frequently than by chance, strongly suggesting an interhemispheric facilitatory grouping mechanism.
evidence: Direct statement about experimental design rationale.

claim: The study replicates that targets sharing color, form, and temporal flicker disappear together more frequently than by chance, strongly suggesting an interhemispheric facilitatory grouping mechanism.
source: We capitalized on this result by designing targets which shared color, form, and temporal flicker, and replicate that these targets disappear together more frequently than by chance, strongly suggesting an interhemispheric facilitatory grouping mechanism.
evidence: Direct statement about behavioral finding and interpretation.

claim: An event-related suppression of alpha-band activity is consistent with spontaneous increases in attention around the time of PFI.
source: Second, an event-related suppression of alpha-band activity is consistent with spontaneous increases in attention around the time of PFI (Figure 3d).
evidence: Direct statement about interpretation of alpha finding.

claim: The same pattern of alpha suppression was not observed for PMD periods, which placed equivalent demands as PFI on report-related motor selection and somatosensory spatial attention.
source: Moreover, the same pattern was not observed for PMD periods, which placed equivalent demands as PFI on reported-related motor selection (van Ede et al., 2019), and somatosensory spatial attention (Anderson and Ding, 2011), suggesting this alpha-band suppression was not related to the mu rhythm.
evidence: Direct statement about control comparison with citations.

claim: The alpha-band suppression was not related to the mu rhythm.
source: Moreover, the same pattern was not observed for PMD periods, which placed equivalent demands as PFI on reported-related motor selection (van Ede et al., 2019), and somatosensory spatial attention (Anderson and Ding, 2011), suggesting this alpha-band suppression was not related to the mu rhythm.
evidence: Direct statement about interpretation with citations.

claim: Across participants, the magnitude of target-SNR increase correlated with the depth of alpha suppression, but only during PFI periods.
source: Third, across participants, the magnitude of target-SNR increase correlated with the depth of alpha suppression (Figure 3e), but only during PFI periods.
evidence: Direct statement about correlation finding.

claim: The IM results indicate a transient increase around the time of PFI disappearance, which peaked between the enhancement of the surround (f2) and target (f1) SNR.
source: Fourth, our IM results (at f2-f1; Figure 4), also indicate a transient increase around the time of PFI disappearance, which peaked between the enhancement of the surround (f2) and target (f1) SNR.
evidence: Direct statement about IM finding.

claim: Previous work has shown that IM-SNR is strongly dependent upon attentional selection of multiple objects.
source: Previous work has shown that IM-SNR is strongly dependent upon attentional selection of multiple objects (Gordon et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2017), which is consistent with attention to the target and surrounds in our PFI paradigm.
evidence: Direct statement about prior findings with citations.

claim: The IM finding is consistent with attention to the target and surrounds in the PFI paradigm.
source: Previous work has shown that IM-SNR is strongly dependent upon attentional selection of multiple objects (Gordon et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2017), which is consistent with attention to the target and surrounds in our PFI paradigm.
evidence: Direct statement about interpretation of IM finding.

claim: The same pattern of IM modulation was not observed during PMD, where target-SNR decreased prior to button press, and was followed by changes to the surround and IM-SNR after button press.
source: The same pattern was not observed during PMD, where target-SNR decreased prior to button press, and was followed by changes to the surround and IM-SNR, after button press.
evidence: Direct statement about control comparison.

claim: Four distinct and convergent lines of evidence argue against alternative explanations such as SSVEP changes due to an increase in global arousal or vigilance.
source: Jointly, these four distinct and convergent lines of evidence argue against other alternative explanations. Other interpretations, such as SSVEP changes due to an increase in global arousal, or vigilance (Silberstein et al., 1990), generally occur over tens of seconds, and so seem unlikely to account for the transient and temporally ordered SNR changes we report.
evidence: Direct statement about ruling out alternative explanations with citation.

claim: Alternative accounts such as motor preparation and somatosensory attention cannot easily explain why both the target and surround-SNR also decrease when targets reappear during PFI.
source: Further, these and other alternate accounts, such as motor preparation and somatosensory attention, cannot easily explain why both the target and surround-SNR also decrease when targets reappear during PFI (Figure 2), as reporting on disappearance and reappearance seem to require similar levels of global arousal and motor preparation.
evidence: Direct statement about ruling out alternative explanations.

claim: It is most parsimonious to invoke an explanation that involves a known interplay between attention and PFI, and a transient enhancement of SSVEP responses due to attention.
source: To explain these target-specific, directionally-specific, and temporally ordered effects, we believe that it is most parsimonious to invoke an explanation that involves a known interplay between attention and PFI, and a transient enhancement of SSVEP responses due to attention, although in the case of PFI, the effect of attentional enhancement is to paradoxically increase the strength of an invisible signal.
evidence: Direct statement of preferred interpretation.

claim: In the case of PFI, the effect of attentional enhancement is to paradoxically increase the strength of an invisible signal.
source: To explain these target-specific, directionally-specific, and temporally ordered effects, we believe that it is most parsimonious to invoke an explanation that involves a known interplay between attention and PFI, and a transient enhancement of SSVEP responses due to attention, although in the case of PFI, the effect of attentional enhancement is to paradoxically increase the strength of an invisible signal.
evidence: Direct statement about paradoxical effect.

claim: Existing theories propose that a combination of activity in the retinotopic visual cortex and higher-level association areas initiate and maintain periods of invisibility during PFI.
source: Existing theories propose that a combination of activity in the retinotopic visual cortex (De Weerd et al., 1998; De Weerd et al., 1995), and higher-level association areas (Dennett, 1991; De Weerd et al., 2006; Kingdom and Moulden, 1988; Pessoa et al., 1998) initiate and maintain periods of invisibility during PFI (Weil and Rees, 2011).
evidence: Direct statement about existing theories with citations.

claim: The study demonstrates that an increase in surround-SNR precedes an increase in target-SNR by approximately 200 ms.
source: Here, we demonstrate that an increase in surround-SNR precedes an increase in target-SNR by approximately 200 ms (Figure 2) and that the temporal order of these activations is consistent across participants (Figure 4).
evidence: Direct statement about temporal finding with figure references.

claim: The temporal order of surround and target activations is consistent across participants.
source: Here, we demonstrate that an increase in surround-SNR precedes an increase in target-SNR by approximately 200 ms (Figure 2) and that the temporal order of these activations is consistent across participants (Figure 4).
evidence: Direct statement about consistency of temporal finding with figure reference.

claim: The timing of significant changes to the intermodulation (IM) component falls between those for the surround- and target-SNR.
source: Moreover, the timing of significant changes to the intermodulation (IM) component falls between those for the surround- and target-SNR (Figure 4).
evidence: Direct statement about IM timing with figure reference.

claim: IM components have been interpreted as an index of the non-linear integration of neural signals, and the existence of neural interactions between sensory stimulus representations.
source: Broadly speaking, IM components have been interpreted as an index of the non-linear integration of neural signals, and the existence of neural interactions between sensory stimulus representations (for review see Gordon et al., 2019).
evidence: Direct statement about IM interpretation with citation.

claim: Changes in IM strength have previously been observed when two visual stimuli compete for perceptual dominance.
source: For example, changes in IM strength have previously been observed when two visual stimuli compete for perceptual dominance (Katyal et al., 2016; Sutoyo and Srinivasan, 2009; Zhang et al., 2011), and to peak prior to a change in conscious percept during binocular rivalry (Katyal et al., 2016).
evidence: Direct statement about prior findings with citations.

claim: IM strength peaks prior to a change in conscious percept during binocular rivalry.
source: For example, changes in IM strength have previously been observed when two visual stimuli compete for perceptual dominance (Katyal et al., 2016; Sutoyo and Srinivasan, 2009; Zhang et al., 2011), and to peak prior to a change in conscious percept during binocular rivalry (Katyal et al., 2016).
evidence: Direct statement about prior findings with citation.

claim: The existence and temporal order of IM activations reveal an important piece of evidence with respect to the neural mechanisms of PFI in human participants.
source: As a consequence, we view the existence and temporal order of IM activations to reveal an important piece of evidence with respect to the neural mechanisms of PFI in human participants.
evidence: Direct statement about interpretation of IM findings.

claim: One key component of low-level accounts is that disappearance is preceded by an adaptation of neurons sensitive to the border between a target and surround.
source: Notably, one key component of low-level accounts is that disappearance is preceded by an adaptation of neurons sensitive to the border between a target and surround.
evidence: Direct statement about theoretical component.

claim: When an achromatic target with a more clearly defined border is filled-in, neural correlates in human V1 and V2 have been identified with fMRI, and BOLD responses reduce in target-sensitive regions.
source: For example, when an achromatic target with a more clearly defined border is filled-in, neural correlates in human V1 and V2 have been identified with fMRI, and BOLD responses reduce in target-sensitive regions in these cases (Mendola et al., 2006; Weil et al., 2008).
evidence: Direct statement about prior findings with citations.

claim: In the current display, boundary adaptation may be reduced because target borders were continuously changed due to the dynamic texture.
source: In our display, target borders were continuously changed due to the dynamic texture that was shared by targets and surrounds (Figure 1c). As a consequence, boundary adaptation may be reduced (Spillmann and Kurtenbach, 1992), and it remains possible that neurons higher in the visual hierarchy with a sensitivity to color (such as in V4) are the neural correlates of PFI in our paradigm.
evidence: Direct statement about stimulus design implications with citation.

claim: The nature of the relationship between attention and consciousness is one of the most hotly debated and empirically examined topics in consciousness research.
source: The nature of the relationship between attention and consciousness is one of the most hotly debated and empirically examined topics in consciousness research (Dehaene et al., 2006; Koch and Tsuchiya, 2007; Tsuchiya and Koch, 2016; van Boxtel and Tsuchiya, 2015; van Boxtel et al., 2010a).
evidence: Direct statement about field context with citations.

claim: Increasing psychological and neuroscientific evidence suggests that attention and consciousness are not supported by the same mechanisms.
source: As reviewed recently (Maier and Tsuchiya, 2020), increasing psychological and neuroscientific evidence suggests that attention and consciousness are not supported by the same mechanisms (see also Norman et al., 2013; Wyart and Tallon-Baudry, 2008; Wyart and Tallon-Baudry, 2009).
evidence: Direct statement about current evidence with citations.

claim: Counterintuitive findings that attention can actually decrease visual awareness in certain situations provide the most direct psychological evidence to argue for the dissociation between attention and consciousness.
source: Among this accumulating evidence, counterintuitive findings that attention can actually decrease visual awareness in certain situations provide the most direct psychological evidence to argue for the dissociation between attention and consciousness (e.g. Ling and Carrasco, 2006; Lou, 1999; Mehrpour et al., 2020; van Boxtel et al., 2010b; Yeshurun and Carrasco, 1998).
evidence: Direct statement about evidence type with citations.

claim: PFI is among the most promising paradigms to examine the opposing effects of attention and consciousness.
source: Along with other perceptual phenomena, PFI is among the most promising paradigms to examine these opposing effects of attention and consciousness (Maier and Tsuchiya, 2020; Tsuchiya and Koch, 2016).
evidence: Direct statement about paradigm utility with citations.

claim: The paper is the first to demonstrate a neural correlate of counterintuitive and opposing effects of attention and consciousness.
source: Building on this prior research, our paper is the first to demonstrate a neural correlate of such counterintuitive and opposing effects of attention and consciousness.
evidence: Direct statement about novelty of contribution.

claim: Perceptual paradigms that manipulate conscious perception tend to confound the effects of attention.
source: As we and others have previously pointed out, however, perceptual paradigms that manipulate conscious perception tend to confound the effects of attention (Aru et al., 2012; Koch and Tsuchiya, 2007; Tse et al., 2005; van Boxtel and Tsuchiya, 2015).
evidence: Direct statement about methodological issue with citations.

claim: Previous uses of the SSVEP technique might have reflected the neural correlates of any or a combination of attention and consciousness factors.
source: Thus, previous uses of the SSVEP technique might have reflected the neural correlates of any or a combination of these factors.
evidence: Direct statement about interpretation of prior work.

claim: When used together with binocular rivalry, SSVEP strength has typically been interpreted as a neural correlate of conscious perception.
source: More specifically, when used together with binocular rivalry, SSVEP strength has typically been interpreted as a neural correlate of conscious perception (Bock et al., 2019; Brown and Norcia, 1997; Cosmelli et al., 2004; Jamison et al., 2015; Kamphuisen et al., 2008; Katyal et al., 2016; Lansing, 1964; Lawwill and Biersdorf, 1968; Roy et al., 2017; Srinivasan et al., 1999; Sutoyo and Srinivasan, 2009; Tononi et al., 1998; Zhang et al., 2011).
evidence: Direct statement about typical interpretation with extensive citations.

claim: Zhang et al. (2011) interpreted a reduction in SSVEP strength to indicate the cessation of binocular rivalry entirely after withdrawing attention from rivalry stimuli, and concluded that 'binocular rivalry requires visual attention'.
source: In one notable study, a reduction in SSVEP strength was interpreted to indicate the cessation of binocular rivalry entirely (Zhang et al., 2011). In their study, Zhang and colleagues obtained this result after withdrawing attention from rivalry stimuli and concluded that 'binocular rivalry requires visual attention' (see also Brascamp and Blake, 2012 for behavioral evidence for this claim).
evidence: Direct statement about prior study interpretation with citations.

claim: A more parsimonious explanation is that SSVEP strength reflects attention, which is typically positively correlated with conscious perception.
source: Another viable, and potentially simpler explanation, is that SSVEP strength instead reflects attention, which is typically positively correlated with conscious perception.
evidence: Direct statement of alternative interpretation.

claim: By opposing the effects of attention and conscious perception, and demonstrating that the strength of target SSVEPs do not capture visual phenomenology, the current results are in line with the interpretation that SSVEPs reflect attention.
source: By opposing the effects of attention and conscious perception, and demonstrating that the strength of target SSVEPs do not capture visual phenomenology, our current results are in line with this more parsimonious interpretation.
evidence: Direct statement about interpretation of current results.

claim: The interpretation that SSVEPs reflect attention but not consciousness is supported by indirect, yet convergent evidence.
source: Importantly, our interpretation that SSVEPs reflect attention but not consciousness is supported by indirect, yet convergent evidence.
evidence: Direct statement about evidence for interpretation.

claim: To test theories that propose certain types of causal interactions underlie conscious phenomenology, consciousness research may need to move away from simple detection or discrimination paradigms.
source: To test these theories, consciousness research may need to move away from simple detection or discrimination paradigms, where the visibility of an isolated object is measured against a uniform background.
evidence: Direct statement about methodological recommendation.

claim: Enriching the sensory input with multiple features and a meaningful background could provide empiricists with a richer repertoire to investigate the interplay of neurons in the visual cortex.
source: Instead, enriching the sensory input with multiple features and a meaningful background could provide empiricists with a richer repertoire to investigate the interplay of neurons in the visual cortex, and, for example, to investigate how the spatial structure of vision arises (Haun and Tononi, 2019; Koenderink et al., 2014).
evidence: Direct statement about methodological recommendation with citations.

claim: By introducing a dynamic texture tagging display, the study has taken a first step toward characterizing the interactions between various visual features based on the strength of SSVEP signals.
source: Here, by introducing a dynamic texture tagging display, we have taken a first step toward characterizing the interactions between various visual features based on the strength of SSVEP signals.
evidence: Direct statement about methodological contribution.

claim: Future work may be able to test whether SSVEPs during PFI at attended/unattended locations replicates the pattern described, using innovative no-report methods to time-lock event-related PFI at unattended locations.
source: To tease apart the neural correlates of conscious phenomenology from those of attention and reports, future work may be able to test whether SSVEPs during PFI at attended/unattended locations replicates the pattern which we have described, using innovative no-report methods to time-lock event-related PFI at unattended locations (Tsuchiya et al., 2015).
evidence: Direct statement about future research direction with citation.

claim: The disappearance of a stimulus and subjective invisibility during PFI is associated with increases in neural activity, as measured with steady-state visually evoked potentials (SSVEPs), in electroencephalography (EEG).
source: We show that in a PFI paradigm, the disappearance of a stimulus and subjective invisibility is associated with increases in neural activity, as measured with steady-state visually evoked potentials (SSVEPs), in electroencephalography (EEG).
evidence: Direct statement from abstract summarizing main finding.

claim: The increase in neural activity during PFI correlates with alpha-band activity, a well-established neural measure of attention.
source: We also find that this increase correlates with alpha-band activity, a well-established neural measure of attention.
evidence: Direct statement from abstract about correlation finding.

claim: These findings cast doubt on the direct relationship previously reported between the strength of neural activity and conscious perception, at least when measured with current tools, such as the SSVEP.
source: These findings cast doubt on the direct relationship previously reported between the strength of neural activity and conscious perception, at least when measured with current tools, such as the SSVEP.
evidence: Direct statement from abstract about implications.

claim: The study concludes that SSVEP strength more closely measures changes in attention.
source: Instead, we conclude that SSVEP strength more closely measures changes in attention.
evidence: Direct statement from abstract stating main conclusion.

claim: Research on the neural basis of conscious perception has almost exclusively shown that becoming aware of a stimulus leads to increased neural responses.
source: Research on the neural basis of conscious perception has almost exclusively shown that becoming aware of a stimulus leads to increased neural responses.
evidence: Direct statement from abstract about prior research.

claim: The study designed a novel form of perceptual filling-in (PFI) overlaid with a dynamic texture display that frequency-tagged multiple disappearing targets as well as their surroundings.
source: By designing a novel form of perceptual filling-in (PFI) overlaid with a dynamic texture display, we frequency-tagged multiple disappearing targets as well as their surroundings.
evidence: Direct statement from abstract about methodological innovation.

claim: A central question in cognitive neuroscience is asking what the neural correlates or constituents of consciousness may be.
source: A central question in cognitive neuroscience is asking what the neural correlates or constituents of consciousness may be (Klink et al., 2015; Koch et al., 2016; Mashour et al., 2020; Miller, 2007).
evidence: Direct statement about field context with citations.

claim: Recent empirical research suggests that various psychological processes, such as cognitive access, expectation, and the act of report, may confound interpretation of neural correlates of consciousness.
source: Recent empirical research suggests that various psychological processes, such as cognitive access, expectation, and the act of report, may confound our interpretation of these correlates (Aru et al., 2012; Frässle et al., 2014; Tse et al., 2005; Tsuchiya et al., 2015; van Boxtel and Tsuchiya, 2015; van Boxtel et al., 2010a).
evidence: Direct statement about confounds with citations.

claim: Task-relevant attention and its relation to visual phenomenology is one of the most hotly debated confounds in consciousness research.
source: Among them, one of the most hotly debated is task-relevant attention and its relation to visual phenomenology (Block, 2011; Cohen et al., 2016; Koch and Tsuchiya, 2007; Kouider et al., 2010; Lamme, 2006; Lau and Rosenthal, 2011; Posner, 2012; Tsuchiya and Koch, 2016).
evidence: Direct statement about debate with citations.

claim: Despite accumulating behavioral evidence in favor of dissociating attention and visual experience, it remains unclear whether the neural mechanisms of attention and visual awareness are distinct.
source: Are attention and visual experience always tightly intertwined, or can they be disentangled? Despite accumulating behavioral evidence in favor of the latter, it remains unclear whether the neural mechanisms of attention and visual awareness are distinct.
evidence: Direct statement about current state of knowledge.

claim: There is still an unmet empirical need for experimental paradigms which can address the question of whether neural mechanisms of attention and visual awareness are distinct.
source: Notwithstanding new methodological developments (Maier and Tsuchiya, 2020; Smout and Mattingley, 2018; Watanabe et al., 2011; Webb et al., 2016), there is still an unmet empirical need for experimental paradigms which can address this question (Pitts et al., 2018; Tallon-Baudry, 2011; van Boxtel, 2017; van Boxtel and Tsuchiya, 2015; van Boxtel et al., 2010a).
evidence: Direct statement about research need with citations.

claim: Perceptual filling-in (PFI) is one candidate paradigm that can potentially dissociate attention from consciousness.
source: Perceptual filling-in (PFI) is one candidate paradigm that can potentially dissociate attention from consciousness.
evidence: Direct statement about paradigm utility.

claim: During PFI, a distinct region of the visual periphery disappears and becomes interpolated by the surrounding image background.
source: During PFI, a distinct region of the visual periphery disappears and becomes interpolated by the surrounding image background.
evidence: Direct statement defining PFI phenomenon.

claim: PFI is a relatively underexplored class of multistable phenomena.
source: PFI is a relatively underexplored class of multistable phenomena (Davidson et al., 2020; Kim and Blake, 2005; Sterzer et al., 2009), but it has distinct advantages over its predecessors (Komatsu, 2006; Weil and Rees, 2011).
evidence: Direct statement about PFI status with citations.

claim: PFI has distinct advantages over its predecessors.
source: PFI is a relatively underexplored class of multistable phenomena (Davidson et al., 2020; Kim and Blake, 2005; Sterzer et al., 2009), but it has distinct advantages over its predecessors (Komatsu, 2006; Weil and Rees, 2011).
evidence: Direct statement about PFI advantages with citations.

claim: PFI has been proposed as a highly promising paradigm to dissociate the neural correlates of attention and consciousness.
source: Since PFI can dissociate attention and consciousness at the perceptual level, in strictly behavioral paradigms, it has been proposed as a highly promising paradigm to dissociate the neural correlates of attention and consciousness as well (Tsuchiya and Koch, 2016).
evidence: Direct statement about PFI utility with citation.

claim: The study demonstrates that PFI indeed dissociates neural measures which normally positively correlate with both attention to, and the conscious perception of, visual stimuli.
source: Here, we demonstrate that PFI indeed dissociates neural measures which normally positively correlate with both attention to, and the conscious perception of, visual stimuli.
evidence: Direct statement about main contribution.

claim: SSVEPs are periodic large-scale cortical responses to rhythmic visual stimuli, 'frequency-tagging' a neural population specific to each flickering stimulus for subsequent analysis.
source: SSVEPs are periodic large-scale cortical responses to rhythmic visual stimuli, 'frequency-tagging' a neural population specific to each flickering stimulus for subsequent analysis (Tononi et al., 1998).
evidence: Direct statement defining SSVEPs with citation.

claim: SSVEPs have a high signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), and as a result have been widely adopted in the basic visual, cognitive, and clinical neurosciences.
source: SSVEPs have a high signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), and as a result have been widely adopted in the basic visual, cognitive, and clinical neurosciences (Norcia et al., 2015; Vialatte et al., 2010).
evidence: Direct statement about SSVEP properties with citations.

claim: During binocular rivalry, dissimilar monocular images presented to each eye compete for perceptual dominance, with conscious awareness typically fluctuating spontaneously between each image.
source: During binocular rivalry, dissimilar monocular images presented to each eye compete for perceptual dominance, with conscious awareness typically fluctuating spontaneously between each image (Alais, 2012; Alais and Blake, 2005; Levelt, 1965; Maier et al., 2012).
evidence: Direct statement defining binocular rivalry with citations.

claim: The study employed a multi-target, multi-response paradigm in which all disappearing targets were matched in color, form, and temporal flicker.
source: We employed a multi-target, multi-response paradigm (Davidson et al., 2020), in which all disappearing targets were matched in color, form, and temporal flicker, and tasked participants to covertly monitor all targets for instances of PFI.
evidence: Direct statement about experimental design with citation.

claim: Participants were tasked to covertly monitor all targets for instances of PFI.
source: We employed a multi-target, multi-response paradigm (Davidson et al., 2020), in which all disappearing targets were matched in color, form, and temporal flicker, and tasked participants to covertly monitor all targets for instances of PFI.
evidence: Direct statement about task instructions.

claim: The neuronal effects of consciousness and attention are expected to be in opposition in this paradigm, if attention to the targets facilitates their disappearance.
source: Thus, the neuronal effects of consciousness and attention are expected to be in opposition in this paradigm, if attention to the targets facilitates their disappearance.
evidence: Direct statement about experimental prediction.

claim: The study developed a novel method that allowed capture of neural markers of attention and/or consciousness during PFI, that separately frequency-tagged targets and their visual surrounds.
source: Importantly, we developed a novel method that allowed us to capture neural markers of attention and/or consciousness during PFI, that separately frequency-tagged targets and their visual surrounds.
evidence: Direct statement about methodological innovation.

claim: The study built upon previous work that has facilitated PFI by making the surrounding regions dynamic, such as when updated with visual noise.
source: We achieved this by building upon previous work that has facilitated PFI by making the surrounding regions dynamic, such as when updated with visual noise (Davidson et al., 2020; De Weerd et al., 1998; De Weerd et al., 1995; Ramachandran and Gregory, 1991; Spillmann and Kurtenbach, 1992; Weil et al., 2007; Weil et al., 2008).
evidence: Direct statement about methodological foundation with citations.

claim: The critical manipulations were to calibrate the dynamic noise texture to evoke an SSVEP and to extend this texture over enlarged target regions.
source: Our critical manipulations were to calibrate the dynamic noise texture to evoke an SSVEP and to extend this texture over our enlarged target regions.
evidence: Direct statement about key methodological innovations.

claim: Target size normally impedes perceptual disappearances during PFI.
source: While target size normally impedes perceptual disappearances during PFI (De Weerd et al., 1998), we included a pre-experiment calibration session to ensure frequent occurrences of large parafoveal PFI for each participant (Figure 1).
evidence: Direct statement about known constraint with citation.

claim: The study included a pre-experiment calibration session to ensure frequent occurrences of large parafoveal PFI for each participant.
source: While target size normally impedes perceptual disappearances during PFI (De Weerd et al., 1998), we included a pre-experiment calibration session to ensure frequent occurrences of large parafoveal PFI for each participant (Figure 1).
